content_html_sanitized:
Posted July 12, 2001
(MarijuanaNews note: One of the most disturbing aspects of the prohibitionist mind is the willingness to take numbers out of context in a way that indicates that whoever did so must have intended to deceive. Once published, they achieve immortality, and are cited again and again. A recent letter to the London Times gave a new example of the misuse of data about the Dutch experience.

Inasmuch as we are apt to see these numbers again, I thought I should address them now. Also it will be interesting to see if the editors of the Times care that they and their readers have been deceived.)

Please allow an American to comment on your cannabis controversy.

Amongst the letters regarding cannabis that you published on July 11th the one from a Mr G. W. Davies says " If the Dutch are so successful in uncoupling the supply of cannabis from that of other, more dangerous drugs (report, July 10), why does the latest report of the European Monitoring Centre for Drugs and Drug Addiction give the following percentages for use by 15 to 16-year-olds? "

He then cites the following numbers, which are indeed in the EMCDDA report:
" Amphetamines: Netherlands, 7.8 (United Kingdom, 7.3); Ecstasy: 8.1 (UK3.0); cocaine: 4.3 (UK 1.5); heroin: 1.3 (UK 0.7). "

As noted, these numbers are from the report, but whoever gave them to Mr Davies surely must have done so with the intention of deceiving him – and subsequently you and your readers.

First, notice that although the subject is cannabis legalization, there are no numbers here for cannabis, a rather odd omission in this context.

In other words, even though cannabis has been available in Dutch coffee shops for decades, the " use by 15 to 16-year-olds " was a full ten percentage points higher in the UK than in The Netherlands.

How is it then that the supposedly higher Dutch use rates for these other drugs is a consequence of the liberal treatment of cannabis, when the Dutch have a lower rate of cannabis " use by 15 to 16-year-olds "?

Second, Mr Davies did not correctly identify these numbers. They do not reflect current " use by 15 to 16-year-olds ", but rather " lifetime prevalence " – having ever used these substances, even just once. This is perhaps the least pertinent number. They are to be found at http://www.emcdda.org/multimedia/Publications/Annual_Report/2000/
data/prevalence/lifetimeprevalenceschoolsurveys.pdf

Third, the numbers he cited were from one of two sets of numbers in the same EMCDDA table. They were immediately below a second set of numbers, which were substantially different. The numbers that he omitted indicated " lifetime prevalence " rates for the same substances that were higher than the Dutch in every case except ecstasy, which was essentially the same:

Amphetamines: 13.0% Ecstasy: 8.0%; Cocaine: 3.0%; heroin: 2.0%

The EMCDDA only says, " Results of the British surveys of 1995 and 1997 are NOT COMPARABLE due to differences in methodology (sampling procedures and questionnaire.) "

However, when we look at more relevant data regarding 12 month prevalence for " young adults " -- 15 to 34 in The Netherlands and 16 to 29 in the UK – results are substantially different.
See
http://www.emcdda.org/multimedia/Publications/Annual_Report/2000/
data/prevalence/last12monthspopulationsurveys.pdf

All three UK surveys show cannabis use rates at least twice that of the Dutch, amphetamine use rates at least seven times the Dutch, ecstasy use rates twice the Dutch, and cocaine use 30% lower in two surveys and twice that of the Dutch in one. There are no numbers for heroin, but, as we shall see, the Dutch have a very low rate of heroin use.

It should be noted that EMCDDA says, " In some countries (United Kingdom) the age range for young adults is more restricted than in other countries, which tends to produce higher prevalence figures. " Thus, the UK situation is not quite as bad as it seems.

However, the real measure of the success of drugs policies has to be in two areas, the first being problematic use.

The July 7th issue of The Economist magazine says, " The Netherlands also has a much lower rate of drug-related deaths - 2.4 per million people, compared with Britain's 31. And whereas in Britain the average age of heroin addicts is 25 and falling, in Amsterdam it has now risen to 36. " In other words, the drug-related death rate in the UK is over ten times that of The Netherlands!

The second measure of the success of Dutch drugs policy is that they have produced these results without arresting the users and retailers of cannabis, while the UK has given criminal records to hundreds of thousands of its young people, creating a chasm of distrust between youth and the police.

The prohibitionists consistently misrepresent the Dutch experience. Former US Drug Czar Barry McCaffrey, was the worst offender. He even claimed that the Dutch murder rate was ten times that of the US, while it is actually less than one fourth the US rate.
See
The Drug Czar’s Testimony On " The Drug Legalization Movement In America " Has Three Parts:
Lie About The Anti-Prohibitionist Movement; Lie About Marijuana; Lie About The Netherlands.
With A Little Lying About Me.
and links

However, given your proximity and long shared history, especially since William and Mary, it would seem that opinion leaders in the UK should be more knowledgeable about the Dutch than we Americans.

Sincerely,

Richard Cowan
MarijuanaNews.com
